newsitem.title: UK: PRESS DIGEST - British Business - June 10.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - British Business - June 10.

text.p: This daily press summary is produced for Reuters by the Broadcast Monitoring Company, which is responsible for its contents. DAILY TELEGRAPH
-- NATWEST MARKETS IN STRATEGIC REVIEW

NatWest Markets has launched a major strategic review of its operations following an unsettled period at the investment bank. Four months ago a 90 million stg 'black hole' was discovered in its derivatives book, and concern has been growing among institutional investors that NatWest is too dependent on volatile earnings streams.
-- SMIRNOFF SHOW TRIAL SHORT OF A TONIC

Grand Metropolitan is to appeal against a ruling from a Russian arbitration court that the brand name for Smirnoff vodka belongs to a descendant of Peter Smirnoff, supplier of vodka to the last tsar. A spokesman for Grand Metropolitan described the Moscow arbitration court as a 'low level' Russian court, and said the company had appealed to a higher court.
-- C&CW TARGETS BT ON PHONE TARIFFS

Cable & Wireless Communications, the new telecoms and cable group formed from the merger of Mercury Communications and three cable companies, has challenged British Telecom over telephone prices by promising to pay a bonus to subscribers who feel they are paying more than BT is offering. The new C&WC tariffs, which include credits for subscribers for double the difference between its own and BT's prices, is available to all new customers who sign up for residential services from June 30.
THE TIMES
-- MARKETS DROP ON FEAR OF EMU COLLAPSE

All of Europe's main stock markets - with the exception of London - suffered sharp falls on Monday as traders became increasingly nervous that the project of a single European currency is about to collapse. On the currency markets, the German mark made strong gains against most European currencies. The fall in stock prices across most of Europe was prompted mainly by comments from the new French finance minister that France wanted more time to examine the single currency stability pact.
-- GRANADA CONFIRMS TALKS

Media and leisure group Granada has confirmed it is involved in talks about a possible takeover of Yorkshire Tyne- Tees Television (YTTV). Following a day of City speculation, the two companies issued a joint statement after the close of trading which confirmed they were in preliminary talks about Granada buying the shares in Yorkshire that it does not already own. Granada currently has a 27 per cent stake in YTTV, although any deal to acquire the rest would need the consent of the Independent Television Commission.
-- MICROSOFT EYES $1 BILLION STAKE IN COMCAST

US software giant Microsoft is set to make its biggest move yet into the media business with the $1 billion investment in Comcast Corporation, America's fourth-largest cable television operator. The deal would give Microsoft a 15 per cent stake in Comcast, which controls cable systems with about 4.3 million subscribers across the US. It would allow Microsoft access to Comcast's distribution channels, offering chairman Bill Gates a key role in shaping the evolution of digital television and interactive programming via the Internet.
THE GUARDIAN
-- BAe FLIES PACT KITE

Senior executives at British Aerospace have floated the idea that political change in France could see a possible merger between BAe and its US rival, GEC, back on the agenda. The executives are concerned that the new French government could delay or scrap the privatisation of defence electronics firm Thomson. BAe and GEC have separate links with the two final bidders for Thomson. If the French also delay the privatisation of Aerospatiale, one of BAe's partners in the Airbus consortium, the way could be cleared for a merger between the UK and US companies.
-- PEARSON PULLS OUT OF DISNEY MAGAZINE DEAL

Pearson is reported to have withdrawn from talks with Walt Disney to buy the US company's Institutional Investor stable of financial magazines. According to 'sources close to Pearson', the UK media and leisure group decided that Institutional Investor would not fit alongside its existing businesses, and that the estimated 123 million stg price was too high. Pearson has refused to comment on the deal.
-- BUSINESS RALLIES TO EMU

Internal research by the Confederation of British Industry reveals that enthusiasm among British businesses for a single European currency is growing, just as events in France and Germany appear to threaten the project. The CBI research is based on a tour of the UK regions, in which the group outlined a series of options for monetary union. Participants say the mood of UK boardrooms has swung in a decidedly pro-Emu direction.
THE INDEPENDENT
-- OUTPUT RISES DESPITE SQUEEZE ON PROFITS

Three separate sets of figures have confirmed the robust health of the UK economy. A survey from the British Retail Consortium revealed that retail sales growth picked up in May, while UK manufacturing production saw its growth in output return to its highest rate for 18 months in April. Factory gate inflation, which rose just 0.1 per cent in April, remained subdued.
-- WINDFALL TAX 'WILL HIKE BILLS' OF HYDER CUSTOMERS

Welsh water and electricity utility Hyder has warned that the government's proposed windfall tax could mean higher bills for its customers. Announcing full-year results which revealed an increase in operating profits from 129 million stg to 284 million stg, the company also warned that the planned levy would mean a cut in spending on cleaning up beaches.
-- DTI SEEKS PETROL PRICE REVIEW

Consumer affairs minister Nigel Griffiths has asked the Office of Fair Trading to look again at whether petrol price wars are driving independent garage owners out of business. The request, which is part of a wider investigation into predatory pricing allegations, follows events last year when market leader Esso apparently lost 200 million stg after sparking a price war with its Price Watch campaign.
